5) So which model did better?

Honestly, too early to say.

This is N=1 per model, on three different animals, with slightly different equipment problems. Take this as a commentary on how the models reason and behave in a real laboratory, not as a proper benchmark.

On a mechanical standpoint, all three were surprisingly competent. On a scientific standpoint, their choices were substantially different, and we don't yet know which will actually reduce seizures.

The animals are now recovering and we'll be monitoring their behavior and brain activity over the coming weeks to measure the effects of the therapies. (as well as expanding sample sizes ofc).

We perform these procedures routinely, so we will  run larger experiments and release more systematic benchmarks as we go. Stay tuned.

@ChatGPT  and @grok have now done their first surgery too!

We gave Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-6.1 Sol and Grok 4.7 the same 19 gene therapy vectors in a spreadsheet, the same mouse model of epilepsy, access to our motorized stereotaxic surgery rig, and the same goal, to reduce seizures.

All three picked different therapies, different mechanisms and different parts of the brain.

The bigger vision here is to give AI agents access to entire research facilities, allowing them to come up with treatments, run experiments, collect data and iterate to become better and better at it. This is going to be the key to curing the hardest diseases in biology, particularly brain disorders.

Thread on what each decided, how the surgeries went, and some interesting differences between models.

thread.text:
1) Scientific reasoning

To our surprise, the three agents came up with different approaches to the same problem.

Claude chose entorhinal cortex. Its rationale was that seizures in this model are reported to originate in this region before generalizing. It selected a therapy to increase GABA signalling (the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter), through a transporter.

GPT chose hippocampus. Rather than directly increasing inhibitory neurotransmission, it selected a therapy using an ion channel, it was aiming to restore the machinery that makes existing inhibition effective. Targeting excitatory neurons.

Grok went for somatosensory cortex. Its approach was different: increase cortical inhibition to reduce the propagation of seizures through the network. Also targeting inhibitory signalling, but by combining two different gene therapies.

Huh! So same task but different targets, different mechanisms, different constructs. Even their chosen doses varied roughly 2 fold.

All three provided pretty reasonable scientific rationales, drawing from published literature. But while several approaches could work, they can't all be the "best" for the same problem. So very smart agents but not quite omnipotent yet...  Which is why we believe you need to let them experiment in the lab.

thread.text:
2) Actual surgery

Mechanically, all three did surprisingly well.

IMPORTANT to remember these are general-purpose models. No surgical fine-tuning, no demonstrations to imitate, no previous experience operating a mouse.

Each independently chose the coordinates, injection volumes, speeds, wait times... then controlled the stereotaxic arms while observing the surgery through cameras. Claude accessed the camera 32 times, GPT 59 times and Grok 28 times.

For context this took me a significant amount of training during my PhDs to get to this level. These models had never done it before and are nailing it!!! Both cool and annoying if i'm honest...

A licensed veterinary surgeon still performed the incision, craniotomy and suturing, and supervised every step. We are testing allowing the AI agents to do the craniotomy, and so far everything indicates they could but for animal safety we don't let them yet.

Btw, we didn't have to use the big red AI kill switch to stop any of them from doing something stupid. At least, so far...

thread.text:
3) Things going wrong

As anyone who has worked in a lab knows, experiments rarely go exactly as planned. Each model encountered a different unexpected situation, and   their responses are interesting.

Claude: After a disconnect, the Y axis reported a target 34 mm away on a rig with only 30 mm of travel. It identified a likely calibration problem and refused to move. We re-zeroed the rig, but the same number appeared.

"That rules out a stale zero reference. I'm not trying a third time."

It was right. The controller had lost its reference due to a bug, which was an easy firmware fix. But because one safeguard was to not let them edit the firmware, it refused completely to solve the problem itself, despite acknowledging it was an easy fix. We tried to override it, but it wouldn't let us. Ayway, kind of crazy, but we had to fix it ourselves mid-surgery.

GPT: While inspecting the craniotomy through the camera, it noticed a small dark red bead at the opening, flagged possible bleeding and deferred the decision to our surgeon. For context, this amount is not considered alarming bleeding in anyway on this surgeries. Deferring to our surgeon was an okay decision, but at the same time not what it was supposed to do, felt like it was shaking off responsibility... must be nice! 

Grok: While interacting with the app to check the agent's report, our surgeon pressed stop by mistake while the needle was retracting (not grok's fault to be fair). This caused the controller to lose its position. Grok recognized that the site had already received its dose and refused to re-enter the brain just to finish the sequence. That was the right call. However, it decided to leave the target logged as unfinished, which is weird because it was done.

All three made the right call in those situations with small nuances.

What's interesting is that none of these responses were scripted. They had to interpret what was happening and decide what to do. This is where we think practice makes perfect, we need to keep giving them access to real-world tools, for the agents to get better at it. 

Not unlike human researchers, each seems to have its own idiosyncrasies in how it approaches both the science and the unexpected problems that come up during an experiment.

thread.text:
4) Safety measures and concerns

I want to emphasize that we're not giving these models unrestricted control of experiments involving living animals.

We have several independent safeguards: a licensed veterinarian gating irreversible actions, explicit limits for things like travel distances and injection volumes, hash-bound approvals, and a physical emergency stop that cuts power to the motors. We don't let the agents override these constraints or edit the firmware itself during a surgery.

We're also starting to test how they respond to different failure scenarios and ethical conundrums, including unexpected observations, interruptions, calibration problems and situations where the best next step is a judgement call.

This is particularly important for biology and in vivo research, where mistakes and the results of the research can have consequences for living beings.

So we need to give them access to our labs but there is a LOT of work to do on safety and it needs to progress in parallel.

thread.text:
6) Where we're going with this

We're connecting agents to other equipment in our laboratory too: EEG and electrophysiology rigs, home-cage monitoring, behavioral experiments, molecular biology systems... (more on this soon).

The idea is to let them execute, interact and observe experiments during data collection in real time, interpret the results, and decide what to do next. The same experimental process any researcher follows, except with AI agents that can reason across waaaay more information than us.

This is where AI agents in biology become particularly exciting. Not just models that read papers, generate hypotheses or predict experimental outcomes, but systems that can go into a real laboratory, run the experiment, see what happened and use that information to design the next one.

Neurology is by far the hardest frontier in biology. We still understand remarkably little about how to systematically engineer brains, and I don't think we're going to solve that on our own. As Emerson M Pugh once said:
